title: Adaptive Batch Sizes Using Non-Euclidean Gradient Noise Scales for Stochastic Sign and Spectral Descent
claim: Adaptive batch sizing driven by geometry-matched noise scales reaches lower loss in fewer steps than constant or mismatched baselines.
layout: 2 panel groups: three line plots left, two geometry sketches right, shared legends
description: Panel (a) has three line plots side by side with a shared x-axis of training steps. The first plot shows validation perplexity falling for small-batch (orange), large-batch (olive), Euclidean adaptive (red) and non-Euclidean adaptive (blue) runs. The blue run ends lowest, near 40. The second plot shows batch size over steps. The adaptive runs step upward, and blue ramps to about 800. The third plot shows the gradient noise scale (GNS). Blue grows to about 300, while red stays low. A wide legend sits below the plots. Panel (b) has two 2-D axes with fans of gray gradient arrows and a bold true-gradient arrow. The first axes bound the arrows with a red circle (Euclidean). The second bound them with a blue tilted square (non-Euclidean). The eye goes first to the colored curves, then to the shapes at right.
caption: In 1a (left), we plot the validation perplexity, batch size, and the exponential moving average of the GNS over steps when training the 160M parameter Llama 3 model for 3.2B tokens on C4 data using signSGD. We compare small-batch (B = 64), large-batch (B = 512), and adaptive batch size strategies based on Euclidean and non-Euclidean GNS. The plots highlight the improved efficiency of using non-Euclidean GNS measurements for signSGD. In 1b (right), we depict how enforcing different GNS (ℓ2 versus ℓ1) changes the geometry of the allowable region for stochastic gradients (with high probability).
abstract: To maximize hardware utilization, modern machine learning systems typically employ large constant or manually tuned batch size schedules, relying on heuristics that are brittle and costly to tune. Existing adaptive strategies based on gradient noise scale (GNS) offer a principled alternative. However, their assumption of SGD's Euclidean geometry creates a fundamental mismatch with popular optimizers based on generalized norms, such as signSGD / Signum ($\ell_\infty$) and stochastic spectral descent (specSGD) / Muon ($\mathcal{S}_\infty$). In this work, we derive gradient noise scales for signSGD and specSGD that naturally emerge from the geometry of their respective dual norms. To practically estimate these non-Euclidean metrics, we propose an efficient variance estimation procedure that leverages the local mini-batch gradients on different ranks in distributed data-parallel systems. Our experiments demonstrate that adaptive batch size strategies using non-Euclidean GNS enable us to match the validation loss of constant-batch baselines while reducing training steps by up to 66\% for Signum and Muon on a 160 million parameter Llama model.
